learn.faqQ2: What level are the lessons designed for?
learn.faqA2: We have content for all levels. Beginners can start with Chess Basics to learn the rules. Intermediate players can improve openings and endgames. Advanced players can develop strategic thinking.
learn.faqA3: Each interactive lesson guides you through concepts step-by-step. You make moves on a real chessboard, get immediate feedback, and can't proceed until you find the correct move. This ensures you truly understand each concept.
learn.faqQ4: Is the learning content really free?
learn.faqA4: Yes! All guides and lessons are free. Create an account to unlock progress tracking, achievements, and learning streaks at no cost.

learn.faqA5: Each track contains multiple lessons and takes several hours to complete thoroughly. But you can learn at your own pace—there's no time limit, and you can revisit any lesson.
learn.faqQ6: Can I skip ahead to advanced content?
learn.faqA6: Absolutely. While we recommend following the learning path in order, you're free to start with any guide or track that matches your current level.

howItWorks.title: How It Works
howItWorks.subtitle: Your complete guide to learning chess on {appName}
howItWorks.heroIntro: {appName} is designed to take you from complete beginner to confident player through structured lessons, tactical puzzles, and real game practice. Whether you want to learn the basics or improve your strategic thinking, our platform provides the tools and guidance you need.
howItWorks.learningJourneyDesc: Follow these steps to improve your chess skills systematically
howItWorks.step1Desc: Start with structured learning tracks designed for your skill level. Whether you're a complete beginner learning how pieces move or an intermediate player refining your strategy, we have a path for you.
howItWorks.step2Desc: Each lesson guides you through concepts with clear explanations and hands-on practice on a real chessboard. Make moves, see immediate feedback, and understand why certain moves work.
howItWorks.step3Desc: Reinforce what you've learned with tactical puzzles. Our curated puzzle packs focus on specific themes like forks, pins, and checkmate patterns so you can sharpen your tactical vision.
howItWorks.step4Desc: Put your skills to the test by playing games. Challenge our AI at various difficulty levels, play with friends, or find opponents through matchmaking. Real games help cement your learning.
howItWorks.step5Desc: Monitor your improvement with detailed progress tracking. See your lesson completion, puzzle accuracy, and rating changes over time. Celebrate achievements and maintain learning streaks.
howItWorks.whatYouCanLearnDesc: Explore our comprehensive learning tracks covering all aspects of chess
howItWorks.featureBasicsDesc: Learn piece movements, special rules like castling and en passant, and basic checkmate patterns. Perfect for those just starting their chess journey.
howItWorks.featureOpeningDesc: Master the fundamentals of chess openings: control the center, develop your pieces, and keep your king safe. Build a solid foundation for every game.
howItWorks.featureEndgamesDesc: Learn critical endgame techniques including king and pawn endings, basic mates, and rook endgames. Knowing how to convert advantages into wins.
howItWorks.featureStrategyDesc: Develop positional understanding, learn to evaluate positions, identify weaknesses, and create long-term plans. Think like a chess player.
howItWorks.waysToPlayDesc: Practice what you learn by playing games in various formats
howItWorks.playAiDesc: Practice against Stockfish, one of the strongest chess engines in the world, with adjustable difficulty from beginner to expert. Perfect for learning without time pressure.
howItWorks.playFriendsDesc: Create a game and share a link with friends. Play real-time games with low latency and see each other's moves instantly. Great for casual games or remote chess sessions.
howItWorks.matchmakingDesc: Find opponents automatically based on rating and preferred time controls. Play bullet, blitz, rapid, or classical games against players at your level.
howItWorks.faqDesc: Common questions about learning chess on {appName}
howItWorks.faqQ1: Do I need to create an account to learn?
howItWorks.faqA1: No! All our educational guides and chess tutorials are publicly accessible. You can read our chess basics, opening principles, and strategy guides without signing up. An account is only needed to track your progress, maintain streaks, and play online games.
howItWorks.faqA2: Absolutely. Our Chess Basics track starts from the very beginning, teaching you how each piece moves, the rules of the game, and fundamental concepts. We designed our lessons to be approachable for anyone who wants to learn chess.
howItWorks.faqA3: Each learning track contains multiple lessons organized by topic. Lessons include clear explanations, diagrams, and interactive exercises where you practice on a real chessboard. You progress at your own pace and can revisit any lesson.
howItWorks.faqA4: Our puzzles are curated by theme, so you can practice specific tactics like pins, forks, or discovered attacks. This focused practice builds pattern recognition faster than random puzzles, helping you spot opportunities in real games.
howItWorks.faqQ5: Can I play without a time limit?
howItWorks.faqA5: Yes. When playing against our AI, you can take as much time as you need to think through your moves. For online play, we offer various time controls including longer classical games where you have plenty of time to consider each move.
howItWorks.faqA6: Yes, the core features are free to use. You can access all learning content, play against the AI, and play with friends without any payment required.

chessBasics.title: Chess Basics
chessBasics.subtitle: Learn how to play chess
chessBasics.heroIntro: Welcome to your chess journey! This comprehensive guide covers everything you need to know to start playing chess. You'll learn how each piece moves, the special rules that make chess unique, and how games are won and lost.
chessBasics.heroDesc: Chess is a game of infinite depth, but the rules are straightforward. Take your time with each section, and soon you'll be ready to play your first games with confidence.
chessBasics.piecesDesc: Each piece has its own movement pattern and strategic value. Learn them all to understand the battlefield.
chessBasics.piecePawnMovement: Pawns move forward one square, but capture diagonally. On their first move, they can advance two squares. When a pawn reaches the opposite end of the board, it promotes to any piece (usually a queen).
chessBasics.piecePawnTip1: Pawns are the soul of chess—their structure shapes the entire game
chessBasics.piecePawnTip2: Central pawns (d and e files) are especially valuable
chessBasics.piecePawnTip3: Connected pawns protect each other and are stronger together
chessBasics.pieceKnightMovement: Knights move in an 'L' shape: two squares in one direction and one square perpendicular. They are the only piece that can jump over other pieces, making them excellent for tactical surprises.
chessBasics.pieceKnightTip1: Knights are strongest in closed positions with many pawns
chessBasics.pieceKnightTip2: A knight on the rim is dim—centralize your knights
chessBasics.pieceKnightTip3: Knights and bishops are roughly equal in value
chessBasics.pieceBishopMovement: Bishops move diagonally any number of squares. Each bishop stays on the same color squares throughout the game. Having both bishops (the 'bishop pair') is considered an advantage.
chessBasics.pieceBishopTip1: Bishops are powerful on open diagonals
chessBasics.pieceBishopTip2: They work well together, covering squares of both colors
chessBasics.pieceBishopTip3: A bad bishop is blocked by its own pawns
chessBasics.pieceRookMovement: Rooks move horizontally or vertically any number of squares. They are most powerful on open files (columns with no pawns) and on the seventh rank, attacking the opponent's pawns.
chessBasics.pieceRookTip1: Activate rooks by placing them on open files
chessBasics.pieceRookTip2: Connect your rooks—having them protect each other is strong
chessBasics.pieceRookTip3: Rooks belong behind passed pawns (yours or your opponent's)
chessBasics.pieceQueenMovement: The queen combines the power of the rook and bishop, moving any number of squares horizontally, vertically, or diagonally. She is the most powerful piece on the board.
chessBasics.pieceQueenTip1: Don't bring the queen out too early—she can be chased
chessBasics.pieceQueenTip2: The queen excels at attacking multiple targets at once
chessBasics.pieceQueenTip3: Avoid trading your queen for lesser pieces
chessBasics.pieceKingMovement: The king moves one square in any direction. While he cannot capture pieces that are defended, he becomes a powerful piece in the endgame when there are fewer threats.
chessBasics.pieceKingTip1: Keep your king safe in the opening and middlegame
chessBasics.pieceKingTip2: In the endgame, activate your king—he's a fighting piece
chessBasics.pieceKingTip3: Learn basic checkmate patterns with your king helping
chessBasics.specialMovesDesc: Chess has three special moves that don't follow the normal piece movement rules. Knowing these is essential.
chessBasics.moveCastlingDesc: Castling is a special move that accomplishes two things at once: it moves your king to safety and activates your rook. To castle, the king moves two squares toward a rook, and the rook jumps over to the other side of the king.
chessBasics.moveCastlingRule1: Neither the king nor the rook can have moved before
chessBasics.moveCastlingRule2: No pieces can be between the king and rook
chessBasics.moveCastlingRule3: The king cannot be in check, move through check, or end in check
chessBasics.moveCastlingRule4: You can castle kingside (short) or queenside (long)
chessBasics.movePromotionDesc: When a pawn reaches the far end of the board (the 8th rank for White, 1st rank for Black), it must promote to another piece. You can choose a queen, rook, bishop, or knight. Most of the time, players promote to a queen since it's the strongest piece.
chessBasics.movePromotionRule1: Promotion is mandatory—you cannot keep it as a pawn
chessBasics.movePromotionRule2: You can have multiple queens (or other pieces) this way
chessBasics.movePromotionRule3: Sometimes promoting to a knight is best (for an immediate check)
chessBasics.moveEnPassantDesc: En passant ('in passing' in French) is a special pawn capture. If an opponent's pawn advances two squares from its starting position and lands beside your pawn, you can capture it as if it had only moved one square. This must be done immediately on the next move.
chessBasics.moveEnPassantRule1: Only available immediately after the opponent's two-square pawn advance
chessBasics.moveEnPassantRule2: Your pawn must be on your 5th rank (or your opponent's 4th rank)
chessBasics.moveEnPassantRule3: The capture is made diagonally to the square the pawn passed through
chessBasics.endConditionsDesc: Understanding how games end is crucial. These are the three most important concepts in chess.
chessBasics.condCheckDesc: When a piece attacks the opponent's king, the king is in 'check.' The player whose king is in check must get out of check on their next move. You can escape check by moving the king, blocking with another piece, or capturing the attacking piece.
chessBasics.condCheckmateDesc: Checkmate occurs when the king is in check and there is no legal move to escape. This ends the game—the player who delivers checkmate wins. Common checkmate patterns include the back-rank mate, scholar's mate, and the queen and king mate.
chessBasics.condStalemateDesc: Stalemate occurs when a player is not in check but has no legal moves. This results in a draw, not a win. Stalemate often happens in endgames when one side has overwhelming material but accidentally traps the opponent's king.
chessBasics.checkmatesDesc: Every chess player should know these fundamental checkmate techniques
chessBasics.mateKQDesc: With just a king and queen against a lone king, you can force checkmate. The technique involves using your queen to cut off squares while your king helps drive the opponent's king to the edge of the board. The queen delivers the final blow, supported by the king.
chessBasics.mateKRDesc: The king and rook checkmate requires more precision but follows similar principles. Use your rook to create a box, shrinking the area where the enemy king can move. Your king must help by covering escape squares. Checkmate happens on the edge of the board.
chessBasics.mateBackRankDesc: A common pattern in actual games. When a king is trapped on the back rank by its own pawns and cannot escape, a rook or queen can deliver checkmate by landing on the back rank. Always give your king 'luft' (an escape square) to prevent this.
chessBasics.nextStepsDesc: Now that you understand how the pieces move and the rules of the game, it's time to learn how to start your games properly. Our Opening Principles guide teaches you the fundamentals that every strong player uses.

cookiePolicy.title: Cookie Policy
cookiePolicy.section1Content: Cookies are small text files that are stored on your device when you visit a website. They help the website remember your preferences and improve your browsing experience.
cookiePolicy.section2Content: RoyalGambit uses cookies for the following purposes:
cookiePolicy.essentialContent: These cookies are necessary for the website to function properly. They enable core functionality such as authentication, session management, and security features. Without these cookies, the website cannot function properly.
cookiePolicy.analyticsContent: We use Google Analytics to understand how visitors interact with our website. This helps us improve our services and user experience.
cookiePolicy.functionalContent: These cookies enable enhanced functionality and personalization, such as remembering your preferences and settings.
cookiePolicy.section3Content: We use services from third parties that may set their own cookies:
cookiePolicy.thirdPartyGA: For website analytics and performance monitoring
cookiePolicy.thirdPartySupabase: For authentication and user session management
cookiePolicy.section4Content: You can manage your cookie preferences in several ways:
cookiePolicy.managingItem1: Use our cookie consent banner to accept or reject non-essential cookies
cookiePolicy.managingItem2: Adjust your browser settings to block or delete cookies
cookiePolicy.managingItem3: Use browser extensions that manage cookie permissions
cookiePolicy.managingNote: Note that blocking essential cookies may affect the functionality of our website.
cookiePolicy.section5Content: Session cookies are deleted when you close your browser. Persistent cookies remain on your device for a set period or until you delete them. Analytics cookies are typically retained for up to 2 years.
cookiePolicy.section6Content: If you have questions about our use of cookies, please contact us at

privacyPolicy.section5Content: We implement appropriate technical and organizational security measures to protect your personal information, including:
